newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks seen opening lower.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks seen opening lower.

text.p: Wall Street stocks are expected to open lower as investors sit tight and wait to take their lead from Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony starting at 1000 EST/1500 GMT.
Market players around the world are will be focusing on hints from Greenspan regarding the odds and timing of an interest rate move in 1997.
"Everything today will be colored by Greenspan's remarks," said Larry Wachtel, analyst at Prudential Securities. "There will be a hesitant tone until he starts speaking."

Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments, said that the market wanted to be reassured by Greenspan that he is ready to move on short-term interest rates at the very first sign of inflation.
"It also wants to be told that such a sign has not yet been spotted, and it also wants to be told that the economy is not falling into negative growth," he said.
"Another important factor upon which he may elaborate is what the consequences are of the strong dollar."
Cardillo said that once the testimony is out of the way the market will go back to looking at eceonomic data.
In Tokyo, the Nikkei Average fell 79.15 points, or 0.42 percent, to close at 18,990.92.
In London, the FTSE 100 Index was up 8.5 at 4353.2.
U.S. shares traded in London were steady to slightly firmer ahead of Greenspan's semiannual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony before Congress.
The dollar weakened against the yen but was off its lows in Tokyo. It was firm against the mark and retracing its losses against the yen in Europe.
U.S. Treasuries were flat to lower, with the long bond down 1/32 to yield 6.66 percent.

The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street writes that a different breed of merger master is back in fashion on Wall Street. Wielding power more subtly, the new breed is doing something that was unthinkable in the 1980s merger boom: buddying up to CEOs and saying they want to develop longstanding relationships.
The New York Times writes that a judge in Deleware gave Marvel Entertainment bondholders permission to foreclose on the bonds and thus take possession of the shares.
